chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Abu Basir, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Qunut (supplication in prayer), and he said: 'In what you recite aloud.' I said: 'I asked your father about that, and he said: 'In all five [prayers].' He said: 'May Allah have mercy on my father; the companions of my father came to him and asked him, and he informed them of the truth. Then they came to me with doubt, so I gave them a ruling based on Taqiyyah (dissimulation/prudence).'

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: Taqiyyah (prudent dissimulation or concealing one's true belief/ruling to avoid harm or confusion)
key_terms.الْقُنُوتِ: Qunut (supplication recited in the second rak'ah of Fajr prayer)

ai.seo_question: Why is the Qunut recited aloud in the Fajr prayer according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the ruling on reciting Qunut aloud in all five daily prayers, highlighting the nuance between the actual ruling (*al-haqq*) and the juristic ruling based on *Taqiyyah* (*al-taqiyya*). Imam al-Sadiq (AS) explains that while his father, Imam al-Baqir (AS), initially taught the companions the truth, he later adopted the practice of reciting it aloud when they returned with doubt, thereby establishing a widely accepted juristic precedent. This illustrates the dynamic interplay between theological truth and practical jurisprudence in Shia legal theory.
